items.originalTitle: Democrats have reached a détente in their internal war. Will it last?
items.author: Lisa Kashinsky
items.title: Democrats have reached a détente in their internal war. Will it last?
items.summary: Democrats’ long-warring ideological factions have reached a détente, new POLITICO Poll data shows . It may not last. Half of progressives and moderates now say the party is “somewhat” or “much more” unified since the election, according to the latest survey, conducted last weekend by PF Global. And everyone agrees on what the Democratic-led Congress needs to do first, above anything else: bring down the cost of living. The size and sweep of Democrats’ midterms romp appears to have temporarily quelled the electability questions that fueled the long-running standoff between the party’s factions. Progressives flipped House districts and snagged Senate seats on plainly purple turf. Many moderate candidates flipped deep-red territory for the first time in decades. Put together, Democrats are now headed for their biggest House majority of the century. “We’ve got this great big-tent party that’s coming into Congress, and I think that’s what people want,” said Pete Giangreco, a veteran Democratic strategist who worked across House, Senate and gubernatorial races this past cycle. “They don’t want these ideological divisions” Today, two out of three Democratic midterm voters believe that progressives make their party stronger — considerably higher than the 41% who said so before Election Day, according to polls taken before and after the midterms. Among self-described moderate Democrats, that belief has risen 26 points, from 33% to 59%. Among progressives, it’s risen from 58% to 74%. “If people are spending more time going after other Democrats instead of figuring out how to work together as a team, then I'm not sure that they've got the right priorities,” moderate Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) told POLITICO. But it’s not clear how long the unity will last. The polling reveals cracks are already starting to reemerge within Democrats’ coalition, foreshadowing potential intraparty fights to come on Capitol Hill and beyond into 2028. Democrats agree on the broad strokes of their priorities, but they diverge on the scope of lawmakers’ approach and the kind of presidential nominee they’d like to see. “Democrats, they don’t need to be getting too big-headed about this quote-unquote blue wave or blue tsunami,” said incoming Arizona 6th District Rep. JoAnna Mendoza. “What they need to focus on is making sure that we’re bringing people relief and that we’re taking action because that’s what people need right now.” The poll bears out two of Democrats’ near-universal takeaways from last Tuesday that are already shaping the shadow 2028 presidential primary: Voters want to elect fighters — and they want them to cut down high costs. The overwhelming majority of Democratic midterm voters — 78% — say bringing down the cost of living should be Democrats’ top focus as they come into control of Congress next year. Nearly as many, 71%, of Americans said the same. But Democratic voters internally disagree on approach. The POLITICO Poll data shows 47% of the party’s midterm voters prefer the next Congress’ agenda be set by Democrats who want major systemic reforms and government intervention to reduce inequality, compared to 39% who prefer Democrats who want pragmatic and targeted economic solutions. A majority of progressives, 57%, choose systemic reform. Moderates, meanwhile, are split between systemic reform (43%) and targeted economic solutions (44%) Those splits are poised to spill onto the presidential campaign trail. Even as voters broadly agree on wanting a “fighter” candidate, half of progressives still think someone with their ideology would be among the most electable in 2028, while just over a third of moderates, 36%, say someone in their lane has the best shot. Several possible White House aspirants are trying to push a public truce, arguing that factional infighting needs to take a backseat for now . "I don't think any voters think about it that way," Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told reporters when asked by POLITICO whether there was a progressive or moderate takeaway from the midterms at Crooked Media's post-election conference in D.C. "People want to see the results of their government because whether you voted for Trump or Harris in the last election, your prices are still too damn high." Progressive Rep. Ro Khanna, in a post-election interview, said “we had electability across the board” in the midterms and that the question heading into 2028 is “who has the best vision for America.” Lauren Fedor contributed to this report.

items.originalTitle: Microsoft Struggles to Repair Worldwide Outage. Here's What You Need to Know
items.author: Tiago Ventura
items.title: Microsoft Struggles to Repair Worldwide Outage. Here's What You Need to Know
items.summary: The icons for a range of Microsoft apps, including Microsoft Outlook, seen on a laptop, in London, England, on Nov. 13, 2026. —Yui Mok—Getty Images An outage affecting Microsoft services including Outlook, Teams, and Copilot has stretched into a second day, leaving businesses and governments around the world struggling to access email communications. Microsoft said that as of Friday morning, users may still “be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services.” While it noted an “encouraging recovery progress in Europe,” with some access in North America “also improving,” it acknowledged that users may still experience “intermittent issues” as recovery actions continue and major gaps persist. “At this time, we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident,” the company stated. Outlook and Teams are widely-used workplace applications, with hundreds of millions of users . The disruption to the services has left some affected workers unable to access their emails, host meetings, or complete other Microsoft-dependent office tasks. Governments and companies impacted worldwide Municipal governments across the United States are still encountering significant system issues, with digital communications interrupted. Baltimore County Government said its staff are "currently unable to send or receive emails due to the widespread Microsoft outage,” but assured the public that 911 and other essential county services had not been affected. The City of Jacksonville, Florida, and City of Austin, Texas, reported similar disruptions to its email capabilities. Tech businesses have also faced disruptions to their day-to-day operations. Users of two leading artificial intelligence companies, OpenAI and Anthropic , reported failures involving Microsoft 365 integration tools. Overseas, the U.K. government said it is still “experiencing problems sending and receiving emails.” The outage also impacted Britain’s National Health Service (NHS), raising concerns about access to appointments and hospital schedules. Some NHS practices have reported not being able to send or receive emails, while others are still assessing the overall impact of the outage. Patients have been advised to make contact via phone rather than using email. As a result, some NHS boards have warned of an increased demand across phone lines. In Japan, lawmaker Masanao Ozaki said the outage had affected the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were “closely watching the company's response.” Meanwhile, the Philippines' Supreme Court warned that “responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed.” In India, the outage disrupted operations at several airlines, with IndiGo and Akasa Air reporting problems related to its customer-support email services. In Australia, federal bodies including intelligence agency ASIO and the Australian Federal Police were affected. Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke reiterated that Microsoft did not believe it was dealing with a cyberattack, suggesting the disruption could instead be related to a faulty software update. "They believe they are dealing in some ways similar ‌to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike, where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke said at a press conference. A major Microsoft IT outage in 2024 grounded flights, sent TV stations off air, and disrupted online hospital systems. The malfunction was linked to a third party, a cybersecurity technology firm named CrowdStrike. The current Microsoft outage began Thursday and peaked in the afternoon, with outage-tracking website Downdetector.com recording nearly 130,000 reports of Outlook problems and more than 45,000 reports involving Microsoft 365 in the U.S. around 1 p.m. E.T. How Microsoft is responding Microsoft has continued to issue updates as its engineers work to restore affected services. The company said it would restart and repair impacted infrastructure, before gradually bringing the services back online. Engineers were also exploring additional measures, such as actively restarting and validating affected servers and using automated recovery systems to find and restart unresponsive servers, in an effort to speed up the process. TIME has reached out to Microsoft for further information. This isn’t the first time Microsoft has experienced an outage. In addition to the 2024 CrowdStrike incident, the company also experienced disruptions affecting Microsoft 365 in January this year and flagged connectivity issues across multiple regions with its Azure cloud platform in October last year.

items.originalTitle: Jordan Firstman Made Club Kid as ‘An Act of Compassion for Myself’
items.author: Rich Juzwiak
items.title: Jordan Firstman Made Club Kid as ‘An Act of Compassion for Myself’
items.summary: Reggie Absolom and Jordan Firstman arrive at the screening of 'Club Kid' on Nov. 2, 2026 in San Francisco, California. —Miikka Skaffari/Getty Images For Jordan Firstman, tears shed during the making of Club Kid would turn out to be a harbinger of success. “I remember getting to the end of the edit, and I would cry every time watching it,” he recalls over Zoom. “My editor would cry every time. Everyone who was allowed in the edit was crying. And so I knew people were gonna be moved.” What the actor, writer, and internet personality did not predict for his feature debut was just how big and immediate that impact would be. It was the toast of the Cannes Film Festival in May. There, the story about queer nightlife and family (chosen as well as biological) received a big standing ovation after its world premiere and, after a bidding war, sold to A24 for a reported $17 million. Six months later, Club Kid has a 98 percent rating on Rotten Tomatoes with more than 100 reviews in. It opened in U.S. theaters Nov. 6 and averaged more than $65,000 per screen—more than stalwart 2026 indies like The Invite , Tony , and Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma . A nationwide expansion is to follow. “I didn't, for a moment, write or make this movie with 75-year-old white men in mind,” says Firstman, though at the Telluride Film Festival in September, he saw even that demographic reacting strongly to his work. “Older people really like this movie and are leaving the theater in tears,” he reports. Club Kid is the feel-good movie of the year, and the copious amount of drugs ingested by its characters are merely a small part of how it’s earned that title. Firstman plays Peter, a toned-down version of the self-absorbed nightmare gay he’s graced both the big and small screens with in recent years (in 2023’s Rotting in the Sun and the HBO series I Love L.A. , respectively). A New York City nightlife veteran who throws parties for a living, Peter is tasked with putting his fast-paced, Ketamine-snorting lifestyle on hold when he discovers he’s the father of a 10-year-old boy whose mother has died. Though he initially rejects the responsibility—he’d completely blocked the memory of having sex with a woman, for starters—Peter is wooed by the intelligent, sensitive Arlo (Reggie Absolom). Despite his limitations, he begins to take his job as a father seriously, which involves attempting to integrate his son into his world, literally bringing him to the club at times. Absolom and Firstman in Club Kid —Courtesy of A24 Firstman filled his film with people he knew from nightlife, and the supporting cast is a major reason why the movie plays so well—its roles feel utterly lived in. The director says he took inspiration from Paul Thomas Anderson’s Boogie Nights , a film in which “everyone with a line has a character.” He made sure there were no negligible roles. “I had talks with every single person in the cast about their backstory, who they are, what they dress like, what they're into,” he says. But the movie simply would not work if Arlo could not charm the audience as readily and fully as he does Peter. “Child actors are hard,” says Firstman. “Some of them feel very extra, some of them feel fake.” Firstman scanned some 100 tapes of potential Arlos and stopped dead in his tracks when he saw Absolom. “That is the face that I was writing in my head—like, he literally had the same face,” says Firstman. “And then I just remember before clicking the link, being like, ‘Please, please be able to act.’” Firstman was struck by Absolom’s naturalism and further impressed when the budding performer picked cuts from Massive Attack and Cocteau Twins from a playlist the filmmaker had sent the prospective Arlos. (“I had them pick out their favorite songs just so I could gauge their taste because I wanted the kids to be cool,” he explains.) And then they met and it was basically settled. “After he auditioned, I turned to say goodbye, and he gave me a look, and I just felt like I knew him. I felt like he was already my friend,” says Firstman. Absolom came to the role by way of sheer ambition. “When I got told I had the first audition, I was like, OK, maybe I can be in my first film because that was one of the goals for me, acting-wise, just to be in a film. And this was such a big role,” says the British actor, on the same Zoom call with Firstman. But the script, which features drug use, public sex, and prolific profanity, gave Absolom, who would be 13 at the time of filming in late 2025, pause: “I was a bit skeptical, if I'm gonna be honest, at first. Like, ‘I'm gonna be around all this?’” Saffron (Saturn Risin9) shows Arlo (Absolom) the ropes on the turn tables —Courtesy of A24 It’s a fair question to ask, and one that the movie itself prompts viewers to pose about its characters: Is this a proper environment for a child? After all, Peter ends up enlisting Arlo, a quick learner on the turn tables, to DJ some of his parties, and while there’s a difference between actually going to a club at 2 a.m. and filming a scene in a club that’s meant to look like it’s 2 a.m., Absolom got more of a taste of underground New York nightlife than possibly any other kid his age on earth. Firstman said he was “hyper aware” of the film’s potential to expose Absolom to inappropriate topics, and fine-tuned which lines would be said in front of the child actor. Absolom says he felt “really well protected” on set. For one thing, his mother accompanied him during shooting. “I understood most of the subjects that were going on, but I just wanted to read through the whole script to understand my character better,” he recalls. “I didn't really need to fully acknowledge what was going on.” For Club Kid ’s kid, shooting the movie was a learning experience. He put the DJing skills he absorbed to use, spinning at the after-party for the film’s Los Angeles premiere. The scene in which Peter’s DJ friend Saffron (Saturn Risin9) teaches Arlo how to use mixing equipment was improvised—Firstman directed Risin9 to abandon the script and just deliver a crash course in DJing. Absolom says he’s interested in clubbing when he’s of age, but “probably not as much as the people in the movie do.” And he’s not interested in drugs. “I'm not gonna do them ever. I don't see a point,” he says. But his biggest takeaway? “I can be friends with anyone, and I like meeting new people and seeing new personalities,” he says. Absolom worked alongside members of the queer community, gay men and trans women alike. He maintains shared streaming playlists with costars David Peck and Risin9, as well as Firstman. As for steering clear of so many of the challenges that have plagued child actors throughout Hollywood history, Absolom is largely focused on attempting not to internalize online negativity. “Most of the things that will happen to a child actor are seeing negative comments and feeling really bad about yourself because of it,” he says. “Right now, I can just block those out.” Together on Zoom, Firstman and Absolom ribbed each other about a fried-chicken dinner at New York’s COQODAQ that Firstman had coordinated for them to get acquainted that never actually happened—Firstman showed up but Absolom didn’t. “I didn't get informed, so I got in the bath,” he says. And Firstman still owes his actor $60 after a promise made on set to give him $20 for each take they needed for a difficult scene in which they both vomit in a pizzeria. “I think when Reggie learned that he could make fun of me, that was a big turning point. Teasing is my love language and people really love to make fun of me,” says Firstman. Firstman knew Absolom was his Arlo as soon as the young actor auditioned —Courtesy of A24 In the film, Arlo integrates seamlessly into Peter’s scene. Part of this is because, in Peter’s words, Arlo is “just so f-ckin’ cool…and you don’t need to do anything at all.” But the turn also functions as effective commentary on the eternal youthfulness of nightlife and the crowd it draws. “No one ever stops celebrating—from age 1 to when you die, you have birthdays, you have family events,” says Firstman. “Celebration is for everyone. And I think the way queer people do it is in a childlike way. You have middle school dances, and I feel like queer people keep that vibe going. We keep that sense of joy alive in us.” For a time, at least. Without giving too much away, Club Kid traces the arc of Peter’s immersion in nightlife to a point where he is decidedly less invested in it, thanks in no small part to his newfound status as a parent. This, in turn, has led to online discourse suggesting that the film is ultimately conservative. Firstman isn’t having it. “I will not entertain the conservative allegations,” he says. “It's just not.” He rejects the notion that his film is “prescriptive,” explaining, “This is Peter's story and Arlo's story, and other characters do keep partying.” He points to a scene toward the end of the film where Peter briefly reunites with a member of his crew. “I tell Saffron to take care of herself, and she says, ‘I always do,’” he recalls. “And that’s my way of saying some people are cut out for this. They can make it work, and they can do it in a healthy way, and they can take care of themselves within the scene. This is a story about a man who couldn't at this time, and he needed to walk away for this moment. But I don't see it as a lifelong decision.” He suggests his character could return to the scene. The fervor that Club Kid has whipped up, positive and negative, is hardly surprising given how strong of a reaction Firstman tends to elicit. He has discussed sensing “a hum of ‘everyone hates me’ for a long time,” despite having nearly a million followers on Instagram alone and several years’ worth of high-profile acting and writing gigs. Club Kid is personal to him not just because he made it, but because he poured himself into it. A scene where Peter describes his low self-esteem to Arlo might as well have been ripped from Firstman’s diary. “I've always been a really social person, and at the same time felt very lonely,” he says. “The part of Peter that I relate to a lot is feeling lonely inside a sea of people. I can have an inflated sense of ego, and I can have crippling [low] self-esteem. Both of those things are true. I think a lot of queer people feel this way a lot, and it's not bad. We've been through stuff, and it's hard to be queer. This movie was an act of compassion for myself.”

items.originalTitle: The Body review – this sexy retro high school drama is like Cruel Intentions … with added Satanic rituals
items.author: Rachael Sigee
items.title: The Body review – this sexy retro high school drama is like Cruel Intentions … with added Satanic rituals
items.summary: This coming-of-age tale of Catholic school girls is gleefully camp from the off – and full of fun references to its 2004 setting. And then a Halloween party goes wrong… What’s more judgmental than a teenage girl? Easy: the Catholic church. Deliciously, Netflix’s new YA drama The Body has both in equal measure. It’s Halloween 2004 at St Mark’s Catholic school and the social hierarchy is exactly as you would expect. Perched at the top is the dance troupe, the Lions, presided over by Anya (Kristina Bogic) and Elise (Sara Boustany), two best friends skirting around their sexual chemistry. The show’s resident outcasts are Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros) and Leo (Jackson Kelly), previously homeschooled siblings who live a limited existence with their unwell mother. Leo seems like a harmless weirdo (or do his disturbing drawings suggest otherwise?) while Lisbeth is a classic loser desperate to ingratiate herself with the cool crowd. Her opportunity arises when she’s invited to a Halloween party at an abandoned convent nicknamed Devil’s House ... what could possibly go wrong? Dressed as “Slutty God” in an attempt to meet the raunchy dress code, Lisbeth heads to the party, where she’s disappointed to learn that a free spot on the Lions team has been filled by Grace (Sofia Wylie), the devout niece of the school’s priest. But when an ecstasy-fuelled, Satan-baiting initiation ritual leaves Grace comatose and the Lions experiencing hallucinations and seizures, the equilibrium of the school is upended.

Guardian science editor Ian Sample tells co-host Madeleine Finlay how this concept usually associated with physics can be applied to conversation, and what the secret to pinkifying our chats could be.

items.title: The datacenter industry is using propaganda to fight opposition | Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
items.summary: Big tech has used misdirection, disinformation and jargon to obscure the harm the facilities can cause to communities “Antifa”. “Commies”. “Chinese bots”. Everyone from tech leaders to the president has called datacenter resistance a “ documented psyop ” and a “ Chinese PR thing ”. But why do they make these claims? Our new research finds that the datacenter industry uses propaganda, disinformation, and information control to mold public opinion and undermine community opposition.

items.author: Oliver Milman
items.title: New York is running out of room for its waste even with Statue of Liberty sized landfill
items.summary: One company is proposing elongating the life of the dump, pungent smell and all, several more decades As a visual representation of how New York is running out of places to put its waste, the largest active landfill in the state is a striking one. The hulking Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty and its operators are seeking to raise it even further, to the consternation of nearby residents. The landfill, situated in the scenic Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state, has grown since the 1980s to now sprawl across 350 acres of deposited trash, mounded up to the height of around 300ft – roughly the same height of the Statue of Liberty.
